name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_STATEMENTMULTI_Q06 - Integrative physiology of micturition accessory excretion and clinical uremia

questiontext.text:
Consider the following five statements (I-V):

Statement I: Filling of the urinary bladder activates mechanoreceptive stretch receptors, transmitting sensory signals to initiate the micturition reflex.

Statement II: Daily human urine contains 25 to 30 grams of urea and normally exhibits a slightly acidic pH of approximately 6.0.

Statement III: Human lungs exhale significant water vapour and eliminate approximately 200 mL of carbon dioxide per hour.

Statement IV: Sebaceous glands eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes in sebum to provide an oily protective barrier for skin.

Statement V: During hemodialysis, blood from an artery is cleared across cellophane membranes into a dialyzing fluid completely free of nitrogenous wastes.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

निम्नलिखित पाँच कथनों (I-V) पर विचार कीजिए:

कथन I: मूत्राशय का भरना यांत्रिक-संवेदी खिंचाव-ग्राहियों को सक्रिय करता है, जो मूत्र-विसर्जन प्रतिवर्त शुरू करने के लिए संवेदी संकेत भेजते हैं।

कथन II: दैनिक मानव मूत्र में 25 से 30 ग्राम यूरिया होता है और यह सामान्यतः लगभग 6.0 का थोड़ा अम्लीय pH प्रदर्शित करता है।

कथन III: मानव फेफड़े प्रतिदिन महत्वपूर्ण जलवाष्प बाहर निकालते हैं और प्रति घंटे लगभग 200 mL कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड का निष्कासन करते हैं।

कथन IV: तेलीय (सिबेसियस) ग्रंथियां त्वचा के लिए एक तैलीय सुरक्षात्मक आवरण प्रदान करने के लिए सीबम में स्टेरोल, हाइड्रोकार्बन और मोम को निकालती हैं।

कथन V: हीमोडायलिसिस के दौरान, एक धमनी से रक्त को सेलोफेन झिल्ली के पार नाइट्रोजनी अपशिष्टों से पूरी तरह मुक्त डायलाइजिंग द्रव में शुद्ध किया जाता है।

उपर्युक्त दिए गए कथनों में से कौन-से सही हैं?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Statement I
Bladder distension stimulates muscular stretch receptors, sending sensory inputs to the spinal micturition center to invoke autonomic detrusor contraction and urethral sphincter relaxation. Therefore, Statement I is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation of Statement II
An adult daily excretes 1.0 to 1.5 L of urine possessing an average pH of 6.0 and containing 25 to 30 grams of urea. Therefore, Statement II is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of Statement III
Human lungs expire approximately 200 mL of carbon dioxide per MINUTE (amounting to 12 L/hour), not per hour. Therefore, Statement III is incorrect.

Step 4: Evaluation of Statement IV
Sebaceous glands discharge sebum comprising sterols, fatty hydrocarbons, and wax esters, forming a protective integumentary shield. Therefore, Statement IV is correct.

Step 5: Evaluation of Statement V
Hemodialysis routes heparinized arterial blood through a semipermeable cellophane dialyzer surrounded by dialysate lacking nitrogenous waste, enabling toxic clearance down concentration gradients. Therefore, Statement V is correct.

Final Conclusion
Statements I, II, IV, and V are correct, while Statement III is incorrect.

चरण 1: कथन I का मूल्यांकन
मूत्राशय का फैलाव पेशीय खिंचाव-ग्राहियों को उत्तेजित करता है, जो स्वायत्त मूत्राशय संकुचन और मूत्रमार्ग संवरणी शिथिलन शुरू करने के लिए संवेदी संकेत भेजते हैं। इसलिए कथन I सही है।

चरण 2: कथन II का मूल्यांकन
एक वयस्क प्रतिदिन 1.0 से 1.5 लीटर मूत्र उत्सर्जित करता है जिसका औसत pH 6.0 होता है और इसमें 25 से 30 ग्राम यूरिया होता है। इसलिए कथन II सही है।

चरण 3: कथन III का मूल्यांकन
मानव फेफड़े प्रति मिनट लगभग 200 mL कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड बाहर निकालते हैं (लगभग 12 लीटर प्रति घंटा), न कि प्रति घंटे केवल 200 mL। इसलिए कथन III गलत है।

चरण 4: कथन IV का मूल्यांकन
सिबेसियस ग्रंथियां सीबम का स्राव करती हैं जिसमें स्टेरोल, हाइड्रोकार्बन और मोम होते हैं, जो त्वचा के लिए एक सुरक्षात्मक आवरण बनाते हैं। इसलिए कथन IV सही है।

चरण 5: कथन V का मूल्यांकन
हीमोडायलिसिस हेपरिनयुक्त धमनी रक्त को नाइट्रोजनी अपशिष्ट रहित डायलाइजिंग द्रव से घिरी अर्ध-पारगम्य सेलोफेन नलिका से गुजारता है, जिससे विसरण द्वारा विषाक्त पदार्थ बाहर निकल जाते हैं। इसलिए कथन V सही है।

अंतिम निष्कर्ष
कथन I, II, IV और V सही हैं, जबकि कथन III गलत है।

answer.text: Statements I, II, and III only
Statements I, II, IV, and V only
Statements II, III, and IV only
Statements I, II, III, IV, and V

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Excretory structures across diverse animal groups

questiontext.text:
Match the excretory structures in Column I with their representative animals in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Protonephridia I. Prawn
B. Nephridia II. Cockroach
C. Malpighian tubules III. Planaria
D. Antennal glands IV. Earthworm

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different animal phyla have evolved specialized excretory structures adapted to their physiological needs for nitrogenous waste elimination and osmoregulation.

Step 2: Structures in Platyhelminthes and Annelids
Protonephridia, or flame cells, are primitive tubular excretory organs primarily concerned with osmoregulation in flatworms like Planaria, rotifers, some annelids, and cephalochordates. Nephridia are coiled tubular structures found in earthworms and other annelids that eliminate metabolic wastes and maintain fluid volume.

Step 3: Structures in Arthropods
Malpighian tubules are characteristic filamentous excretory organs found in insects including cockroaches. Antennal glands, also called green glands, perform excretory and osmoregulatory roles in crustaceans such as prawns.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Protonephridia with Planaria, Nephridia with Earthworm, Malpighian tubules with Cockroach, and Antennal glands with Prawn.

answer.text: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Modes of excretion and animal representatives

questiontext.text:
Match the excretory nature or organism in Column I with the correct description or category in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Ammonotelism I. Protonephridia
B. Terrestrial amphibians II. Uricotelism
C. Reptiles and birds III. Many bony fishes
D. Cephalochordate Amphioxus IV. Ureotelism

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The nature of nitrogenous waste excreted by an animal depends largely on water availability and habitat, dividing animals into ammonotelic, ureotelic, and uricotelic forms.

Step 2: Analysis of Ammonotelism and Ureotelism
Ammonotelism is observed in aquatic organisms such as many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, and aquatic insects where ammonia readily diffuses across body or gill surfaces. Terrestrial adaptations led to ureotelism in mammals, many terrestrial amphibians, and marine fishes, converting ammonia to less toxic urea in the liver.

Step 3: Analysis of Uricotelism and Primitive Excretory Units
Reptiles, birds, land snails, and insects excrete uric acid as pellets or paste with minimal water loss, exhibiting uricotelism. Amphioxus is a cephalochordate that relies on protonephridia for osmoregulation and ionic balance.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Ammonotelism with Many bony fishes, Terrestrial amphibians with Ureotelism, Reptiles and birds with Uricotelism, and Cephalochordate Amphioxus with Protonephridia.

answer.text: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I
A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - Segments of nephron and their functions

questiontext.text:
Match the segments of the human nephron in Column I with their primary functional attributes in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Proximal convoluted tubule I. Permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes
B. Descending limb of Henle's loop II. Conditional reabsorption of sodium ions and water
C. Ascending limb of Henle's loop III. Reabsorption of 70 to 80 percent of electrolytes and water
D. Distal convoluted tubule IV. Impermeable to water but allows active or passive transport of electrolytes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different segments of the nephron possess specialized epithelial linings that determine differential permeability to water and electrolytes.

Step 2: Convoluted Tubule Functions
The proximal convoluted tubule is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium that increases surface area, reabsorbing nearly all essential nutrients along with 70 to 80 percent of electrolytes and water. The distal convoluted tubule carries out conditional reabsorption of sodium ions and water regulated by hormones.

Step 3: Permeability of Henle's Loop Limbs
The descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, leading to concentration of the filtrate as it descends. The ascending limb is impermeable to water but allows active or passive transport of electrolytes, diluting the filtrate as it ascends.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Proximal convoluted tubule with reabsorption of 70 to 80 percent of electrolytes and water, Descending limb of Henle's loop with permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, Ascending limb of Henle's loop with impermeable to water but allows active or passive transport of electrolytes, and Distal convoluted tubule with conditional reabsorption of sodium ions and water.

answer.text: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III
A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Hormonal regulators of human kidney function

questiontext.text:
Match the regulatory hormones or factors in Column I with their specific physiological actions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Antidiuretic hormone I. Converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I
B. Renin II. Causes vasodilation and checks renin-angiotensin mechanism
C. Aldosterone III. Facilitates water reabsorption from latter parts of the tubule
D. Atrial natriuretic factor IV. Stimulates reabsorption of sodium ions and water from distal tubule

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kidney function is regulated by integrated feedback loops involving the hypothalamus, juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), adrenal cortex, and the heart.

Step 2: Hypothalamic and JGA Mediators
Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), released from the neurohypophysis in response to hyperosmolarity or fluid loss, acts on the latter parts of the tubule to promote water reabsorption and prevent diuresis. A decline in glomerular blood flow or pressure triggers juxtaglomerular cells to secrete renin, which converts circulating angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

Step 3: Adrenal and Cardiac Regulators
Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which drives reabsorption of sodium ions and water from distal renal tubules. In response to high atrial blood flow, the heart secretes atrial natriuretic factor, which causes vasodilation, lowers blood pressure, and antagonizes the renin-angiotensin pathway.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Antidiuretic hormone with facilitates water reabsorption from latter parts of the tubule, Renin with converts angiotensinogen in blood to angiotensin I, Aldosterone with stimulates reabsorption of sodium ions and water from distal tubule, and Atrial natriuretic factor with causes vasodilation and checks renin-angiotensin mechanism.

answer.text: A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III
A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q05 - Clinical disorders of the excretory system

questiontext.text:
Match the clinical conditions and disorders in Column I with their correct descriptions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Uremia I. Inflammation of the glomeruli of kidney
B. Renal calculi II. Presence of glucose in urine indicating diabetes mellitus
C. Glomerulonephritis III. Accumulation of urea in blood due to kidney malfunction
D. Glycosuria IV. Insoluble mass of crystallised salts like oxalates formed within the kidney

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Excretory system malfunctions and metabolic imbalances produce specific clinical syndromes and diagnostic urinalysis findings.

Step 2: Renal Pathologies
Uremia occurs when kidney failure causes accumulation of urea in the blood, necessitating hemodialysis or renal transplantation. Renal calculi refer to stones or insoluble crystalline masses of salts, such as oxalates, formed inside the kidney. Glomerulonephritis is an inflammatory disease affecting the glomeruli of the kidneys.

Step 3: Urinalysis Indicators
The excretion of glucose in urine is termed glycosuria, which, when accompanied by ketone bodies (ketonuria), is a clinical hallmark of diabetes mellitus.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Uremia with accumulation of urea in blood due to kidney malfunction, Renal calculi with insoluble mass of crystallised salts like oxalates formed within the kidney, Glomerulonephritis with inflammation of the glomeruli of kidney, and Glycosuria with presence of glucose in urine indicating diabetes mellitus.

answer.text: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q06 - Accessory excretory organs and eliminated substances

questiontext.text:
Match the accessory excretory organs or glands in Column I with their characteristic excretory secretions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Lungs I. Sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes in sebum
B. Liver II. Watery fluid containing sodium chloride, small amounts of urea, and lactic acid
C. Sweat glands III. Elimination of approximately 200 mL of carbon dioxide per minute
D. Sebaceous glands IV. Secretion containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, and degraded steroid hormones

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Apart from kidneys, organs such as the lungs, liver, and skin assist significantly in excreting volatile, lipid-soluble, or metabolic wastes from the human body.

Step 2: Internal Excretory Organs
Human lungs eliminate approximately 200 mL of carbon dioxide per minute along with water vapor. The liver secretes bile pigments including bilirubin and biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins, and drugs that are eliminated with digestive feces.

Step 3: Cutaneous Glands
Sweat glands produce a watery solution containing sodium chloride, traces of urea, and lactic acid, serving primary cooling and secondary excretory roles. Sebaceous glands eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes via sebum, creating a protective oily skin coating.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Lungs with elimination of approximately 200 mL of carbon dioxide per minute, Liver with secretion containing bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, and degraded steroid hormones, Sweat glands with watery fluid containing sodium chloride, small amounts of urea, and lactic acid, and Sebaceous glands with sterols, hydrocarbons, and waxes in sebum.

answer.text: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV
A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q07 - Structural components of human kidney anatomy

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical structures of the human kidney in Column I with their precise anatomical features in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Hilum I. Broad funnel-shaped space with calyces inner to the hilum
B. Renal pelvis II. Cortical tissue extending between medullary pyramids
C. Columns of Bertini III. Notch on inner concave surface where ureter, vessels, and nerves enter
D. Podocytes IV. Specialized epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule with filtration slits

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human kidney contains distinct macroscopic landmarks and microscopic cellular adaptations facilitating blood entry, filtration, and urine collection.

Step 2: Gross Anatomical Architecture
The hilum is a notch on the medial concave surface through which the ureter, renal blood vessels, and nerves pass. Directly inner to the hilum lies the renal pelvis, a broad funnel-shaped chamber with calyces collecting urine from medullary pyramids. The renal cortex projects inward between adjacent medullary pyramids as the Columns of Bertini.

Step 3: Microscopic Epithelial Architecture
Podocytes are complex epithelial cells of the inner visceral wall of Bowman's capsule that form filtration slits (slit pores) to permit fine ultrafiltration of plasma.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Hilum with notch on inner concave surface where ureter, vessels, and nerves enter, Renal pelvis with broad funnel-shaped space with calyces inner to the hilum, Columns of Bertini with cortical tissue extending between medullary pyramids, and Podocytes with specialized epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule with filtration slits.

answer.text: A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV
A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q08 - Countercurrent mechanisms and medullary concentration gradient

questiontext.text:
Match the components of the countercurrent mechanism in Column I with their specific solute transport roles in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Ascending limb of Henle's loop I. Returns sodium chloride back to the medullary interstitium
B. Descending limb of vasa recta II. Allows small amounts of urea into medullary interstitium to maintain osmolarity
C. Ascending limb of vasa recta III. Transports sodium chloride that is exchanged with descending limb of vasa recta
D. Collecting duct IV. Takes up sodium chloride from medullary interstitium as blood flows downward

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The countercurrent multiplier system of Henle's loop and exchanger system of vasa recta maintain an osmolar gradient increasing from \(300\text{ mOsmol L}^{-1}\) in the cortex to \(1200\text{ mOsmol L}^{-1}\) in the inner medulla, primarily via sodium chloride and urea recycling.

Step 2: Transport in Henle's Loop and Vasa Recta
Sodium chloride transported out by the ascending limb of Henle's loop enters the descending limb of the vasa recta. As blood ascends towards the cortex through the ascending limb of the vasa recta, this sodium chloride is returned back to the medullary interstitium, preventing medullary solute depletion.

Step 3: Transport in Collecting Duct
Small amounts of urea enter the thin ascending limb of Henle's loop and are recycled back to the inner medullary interstitium through the collecting duct, preserving high hypertonicity.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Ascending limb of Henle's loop with transports sodium chloride that is exchanged with descending limb of vasa recta, Descending limb of vasa recta with takes up sodium chloride from medullary interstitium as blood flows downward, Ascending limb of vasa recta with returns sodium chloride back to the medullary interstitium, and Collecting duct with allows small amounts of urea into medullary interstitium to maintain osmolarity.

answer.text: A-I, B-IV, C-III, D-II
A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q09 - Transport processes during human urine formation

questiontext.text:
Match the physiological transport mechanisms in Column I with their appropriate functional descriptions in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Glomerular ultrafiltration I. Movement of water in initial segments and nitrogenous wastes along concentration gradients
B. Active tubular reabsorption II. Secretion of hydrogen ions, potassium ions, and ammonia to maintain acid-base balance
C. Passive tubular reabsorption III. Non-selective filtration of plasma except proteins across three layers driven by capillary pressure
D. Tubular secretion IV. Selective carrier-mediated uptake of glucose, amino acids, and sodium ions against gradients

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Urine formation relies on three integrated processes: non-selective glomerular ultrafiltration, selective active/passive tubular reabsorption, and active tubular secretion.

Step 2: Filtration Mechanics
Glomerular ultrafiltration is driven by glomerular capillary blood pressure filtering blood through the capillary endothelium, basement membrane, and podocyte slit pores, allowing all plasma constituents except proteins into Bowman's space.

Step 3: Reabsorption and Secretion Pathways
Substances like glucose, amino acids, and sodium ions undergo active tubular reabsorption against concentration gradients, whereas water in early segments and nitrogenous wastes are reabsorbed passively down concentration gradients. Tubular secretion selectively moves hydrogen ions, potassium ions, and ammonia into the filtrate to maintain body fluid pH and electrolyte balance.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Glomerular ultrafiltration with non-selective filtration of plasma except proteins across three layers driven by capillary pressure, Active tubular reabsorption with selective carrier-mediated uptake of glucose, amino acids, and sodium ions against gradients, Passive tubular reabsorption with movement of water in initial segments and nitrogenous wastes along concentration gradients, and Tubular secretion with secretion of hydrogen ions, potassium ions, and ammonia to maintain acid-base balance.

answer.text: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II
A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q10 - Physiological values in human renal functioning

questiontext.text:
Match the physiological parameters in Column I with their standard normal values in Column II:

Column I Column II
A. Glomerular filtration rate per day I. \(25\text{ to }30\text{ g}\)
B. Renal blood filtration per minute II. \(180\text{ litres}\)
C. Daily excretion of urea in adult human III. \(200\text{ mL}\)
D. Carbon dioxide eliminated by lungs per minute IV. \(1100\text{ to }1200\text{ mL}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Physiological Constants
Quantitative values defined in human physiology characterize standard filtration rates, blood throughput, and excretory elimination capacities.

Step 2: Renal Perfusion and Ultrafiltration Volumes
In a healthy adult, kidneys filter approximately \(1100\text{ to }1200\text{ mL}\) of blood per minute, which accounts for roughly one-fifth of cardiac output. The glomerular filtration rate is about \(125\text{ mL/min}\), which totals \(180\text{ litres}\) of filtrate formed per day.

Step 3: Excretory Turnover Values
Out of the filtered volume, about \(99\%\) is reabsorbed, resulting in \(1\text{ to }1.5\text{ litres}\) of urine containing an average of \(25\text{ to }30\text{ g}\) of urea excreted per day. Additionally, the lungs remove approximately \(200\text{ mL}\) of carbon dioxide each minute.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct matching pairs Glomerular filtration rate per day with \(180\text{ litres}\), Renal blood filtration per minute with \(1100\text{ to }1200\text{ mL}\), Daily excretion of urea in adult human with \(25\text{ to }30\text{ g}\), and Carbon dioxide eliminated by lungs per minute with \(200\text{ mL}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q01 - Sequence of events in micturition reflex

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following physiological events occurring during the micturition reflex in the correct chronological sequence:

  1. Stretch receptors on the wall of the urinary bladder send afferent signals to the Central Nervous System (CNS).
  2. Urine progressively accumulates in the urinary bladder, leading to stretching of the bladder wall.
  3. Smooth muscles of the urinary bladder contract while the urethral sphincter relaxes simultaneously.
  4. The CNS processes the afferent input and transmits motor messages to the urinary bladder.
  5. Release and expulsion of urine occurs through the urethra.

Choose the correct option representing the proper sequence:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Micturition is the neural reflex mechanism by which urine temporarily stored in the urinary bladder is expelled under coordinated voluntary and autonomic control.

Step 2: Sensory Activation Sequence
Urine formed continuously by the nephrons enters the urinary bladder via the ureters. As the volume of urine increases, the bladder wall stretches progressively. This physical distension stimulates stretch receptors embedded within the bladder wall, which generate action potentials that travel as afferent sensory signals to the Central Nervous System (CNS).

Step 3: Motor Response and Efferent Action
Upon integrating the sensory input, the CNS generates motor impulses that travel via autonomic efferent pathways to the effector tissues. These signals initiate the contraction of the smooth muscles of the bladder body and cause simultaneous relaxation of the urethral sphincter guarding the bladder neck.

Step 4: Mechanical Expulsion
The resulting rise in intravesical pressure overcomes urethral resistance, culminating in the outflow and release of urine through the urethra.

Step 5: Final Answer
The correct physiological order begins with urine accumulation and stretching of the bladder wall, followed by activation of stretch receptors sending signals to the CNS, then transmission of motor messages from the CNS, subsequent contraction of bladder smooth muscle with simultaneous relaxation of the urethral sphincter, and finally the expulsion of urine through the urethra (II → I → IV → III → V).

answer.text: I → II → IV → III → V
II → I → IV → III → V
II → I → III → IV → V
I → IV → II → III → V

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q02 - Sequence of renin angiotensin aldosterone activation pathway

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following physiological steps of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone mechanism in the correct chronological sequence following an acute reduction in body fluid volume:

  1. Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells get activated to secrete the enzyme renin into systemic circulation.
  2. Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to synthesize and release aldosterone.
  3. A decrease occurs in glomerular blood flow, glomerular blood pressure, or glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
  4. Aldosterone drives conditional reabsorption of Na\(^+\) and water from distal segments of the nephron.
  5. Renin enzymatically converts plasma angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.
  6. Angiotensin I is further converted into the powerful vasoconstrictor angiotensin II.

Choose the correct sequence from the options below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis operates as an essential neuroendocrine autoregulatory feedback loop to restore arterial blood pressure, renal perfusion, and glomerular filtration rate when hypovolemia or hypotension occurs.

Step 2: Sensory Trigger and Renin Release
A decrease in systemic blood volume or renal perfusion pressure manifests as a reduction in glomerular blood flow, glomerular capillary blood pressure, or GFR. This hemodynamic decline serves as the initial trigger sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus, prompting JG cells to release renin into the bloodstream.

Step 3: Enzymatic Cascade and Angiotensin II Production
Circulating renin cleaves hepatic angiotensinogen into decapeptide angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is subsequently converted into octapeptide angiotensin II, which exerts potent systemic vasoconstriction to elevate perfusion pressure.

Step 4: Endocrine Release and Tubular Reabsorption
Angiotensin II acts upon the adrenal cortex, stimulating the secretion of the mineralocorticoid hormone aldosterone. Aldosterone acts directly on the principal cells of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct to enhance the reabsorption of sodium ions and water into the peritubular capillaries, thereby restoring intravascular volume and returning GFR back to homeostatic levels.

Step 5: Final Answer
The chronological sequence starts with a fall in glomerular flow/pressure/GFR, followed by JG cell activation releasing renin, conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, release of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex, and ends with aldosterone-mediated reabsorption of Na\(^+\) and water from the distal nephron (III → I → V → VI → II → IV).

answer.text: I → III → V → VI → II → IV
III → I → VI → V → II → IV
III → I → V → VI → II → IV
III → V → I → VI → IV → II

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q01 - Excretion of ammonia in aquatic animals

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups of animals is predominantly ammonotelic?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Principle of Ammonotelism
Ammonotelism is the process of excreting nitrogenous waste primarily in the form of ammonia. Ammonia is highly toxic and readily soluble in water, requiring abundant water for rapid elimination.

Step 2: Organism Distribution
Bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, and aquatic insects live in aquatic environments with ample water availability. They eliminate ammonia mainly by diffusion across body surfaces or gill surfaces as ammonium ions, where kidneys do not play a significant excretory role.

Step 3: Comparison with Other Taxa
Terrestrial animals such as mammals and terrestrial amphibians conserve water by converting ammonia to urea (ureotelism). Reptiles, birds, and land snails convert ammonia to uric acid (uricotelism) to minimise water loss.

Final Conceptual Answer: Bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, and aquatic insects are predominantly ammonotelic.

answer.text: Mammals, terrestrial amphibians, and marine fishes
Bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, and aquatic insects
Reptiles, birds, land snails, and terrestrial insects
Cartilaginous fishes, desert mammals, and birds

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q02 - Excretion of uric acid as pellet or paste

questiontext.text: Which of the following forms of nitrogenous waste is the least toxic and can be excreted with minimum loss of water in the form of a pellet or paste?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Comparative Nitrogenous Wastes
Animals excrete three major forms of nitrogenous wastes: ammonia, urea, and uric acid. Toxicity levels rank as ammonia being the most toxic, urea of intermediate toxicity, and uric acid being the least toxic.

Step 2: Water Conservation Mechanism
Because uric acid is least toxic and largely insoluble in water, it precipitates out and can be eliminated with minimal water expenditure. Uricotelic organisms like reptiles, birds, land snails, and insects void uric acid as a semi-solid pellet or paste.

Final Conceptual Answer: Uric acid is the least toxic nitrogenous waste and is excreted as a pellet or paste with minimum water loss.

answer.text: Ammonia
Urea
Uric acid
Creatinine

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q03 - Site of urea production from ammonia

questiontext.text: In ureotelic animals like mammals, ammonia produced by metabolism is converted into urea predominantly in which organ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Metabolic Origin and Detoxification
Ammonia is produced continuously as a toxic byproduct of protein deamination and amino acid metabolism throughout the body.

Step 2: Hepatic Conversion
In ureotelic animals such as mammals and adult terrestrial amphibians, ammonia is transported to the liver, where biochemical pathways convert it into the far less toxic molecule urea. The urea is subsequently released into the bloodstream to be filtered and excreted by the kidneys.

Final Conceptual Answer: Ammonia is converted into urea predominantly in the liver.

answer.text: Kidneys
Liver
Urinary bladder
Spleen

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q04 - Primary function of protonephridia or flame cells

questiontext.text: Protonephridia, or flame cells, found in Platyhelminthes, rotifers, and Amphioxus, are primarily concerned with which physiological process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Invertebrate Excretory Structures
Protonephridia (flame cells) are primitive tubular excretory units characteristic of flatworms like Planaria, rotifers, some annelids, and cephalochordates like Amphioxus.

Step 2: Physiological Role
While they assist in removing waste, their primary evolutionary and physiological role is maintaining proper water and ionic balance (osmoregulation) within the organism's body fluids.

Final Conceptual Answer: Protonephridia or flame cells are primarily concerned with ionic and fluid volume regulation (osmoregulation).

answer.text: Active reabsorption of urea into body fluids
Direct ultrafiltration under hydrostatic arterial pressure
Ionic and fluid volume regulation (osmoregulation)
Production of concentrated hypertonic uric acid pellets

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q05 - Excretory structures in crustaceans and insects

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly pairs an invertebrate group with its designated excretory structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Survey of Animal Excretory Structures
Invertebrates possess varied specialized tubular structures. Flatworms possess protonephridia (flame cells). Earthworms and annelids possess nephridia.

Step 2: Arthropod Adaptations
Within arthropods, crustaceans such as prawns utilize antennal glands, also known as green glands. Terrestrial insects such as cockroaches possess Malpighian tubules that empty into the digestive tract.

Final Conceptual Answer: Crustaceans like prawns have antennal glands (green glands), while insects have Malpighian tubules.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q06 - Dual function of nephridia in annelids

questiontext.text: What is the functional significance of nephridia in earthworms and other annelids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structure and Location
Nephridia are coiled, segmentally arranged tubular excretory structures present in earthworms and various annelids.

Step 2: Functional Role
Nephridia open into the coelom to collect fluid, selectively absorb required solutes and water, and void excess nitrogenous wastes while maintaining proper fluid volume and ionic homeostasis.

Final Conceptual Answer: Nephridia eliminate nitrogenous wastes and maintain fluid and ionic balance.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q07 - Retention of urea in kidney matrix

questiontext.text: Why is a certain amount of urea retained in the medullary interstitium of some ureotelic animals?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Urea Cycling and Retention
Although urea is a metabolic waste product, not all of it is immediately voided in the urine.

Step 2: Osmotic Gradient Role
Some amount of urea is deliberately retained within the kidney matrix (medullary interstitium). Along with sodium chloride, this retained urea generates and maintains the high medullary osmolarity necessary for osmotic extraction of water from the collecting duct.

Final Conceptual Answer: Urea is retained to maintain a desired osmolarity in the medullary interstitium for water reabsorption.

To prevent the entry of sodium and chloride ions into Henle's loop

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q08 - Comparative toxicity and water requirements of wastes

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly evaluates the relationship between toxicity and water requirements for the excretion of common nitrogenous wastes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Toxicity Hierarchy
Ammonia is highly toxic because it interferes with cellular respiration and neural signaling. Urea is significantly less toxic, and uric acid has very low toxicity and is practically insoluble in water.

Step 2: Hydration Costs
Due to high toxicity, ammonia must be diluted in very large volumes of water (approximately 300 to 500 mL per gram of nitrogen). In contrast, uric acid precipitates as a paste or pellet, requiring as little as 10 mL of water per gram of nitrogen.

Final Conceptual Answer: Ammonia is the most toxic and requires the greatest volume of water, whereas uric acid is the least toxic and requires the minimum volume of water.

answer.text: Urea is the most toxic nitrogenous waste and requires large volumes of water compared to ammonia
Uric acid is the most toxic and requires the greatest volume of water, whereas ammonia is the least toxic
Ammonia and uric acid share identical toxicity and water requirements for excretion
Ammonia is the most toxic and requires the greatest volume of water, whereas uric acid is the least toxic and requires the minimum volume of water

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q09 - Vertebral location of human kidneys

questiontext.text: In an adult human, where are the kidneys anatomically situated relative to the vertebral column?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Anatomical Landmarks
In humans, the paired reddish-brown, bean-shaped kidneys lie retroperitoneally along the posterior abdominal wall.

Step 2: Vertebral Alignment
The exact anatomical span corresponds to the level from the last thoracic vertebra (T12) to the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

Final Conceptual Answer: The kidneys are situated between the levels of the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q10 - Dimensions and weight of adult human kidney

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of measurements represents the typical dimensions and average weight of each kidney in an adult human?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Standard Metric Values
An adult human kidney measures 10 to 12 cm in length, 5 to 7 cm in width, and 2 to 3 cm in thickness.

Step 2: Gravimetric Range
The average mass of an adult human kidney is 120 to 170 g.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q11 - Gross internal anatomy of the human kidney

questiontext.text: Towards the centre of the inner concave surface of the kidney is a notch called the hilum. What broad funnel-shaped space lies immediately internal to the hilum?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Hilum Architecture
The inner concave surface of the kidney has a central notch termed the hilum, serving as the entry/exit route for the ureter, renal blood vessels, and nerves.

Step 2: Renal Pelvis and Calyces
Inner to the hilum lies a broad funnel-shaped space called the renal pelvis. The renal pelvis gives off branch-like projections called calyces, into which the medullary pyramids project.

Final Conceptual Answer: Inner to the hilum lies the broad funnel-shaped renal pelvis with projections called calyces.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q12 - Structural identity of Columns of Bertini

questiontext.text: What anatomical structures in the human kidney are designated as the Columns of Bertini (renal columns)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Zonation of Kidney
The interior of the human kidney is divided into an outer cortex and an inner medulla. The medulla is organized into conical masses known as medullary pyramids.

Step 2: Cortical Projections
The cortex extends into the medullary region between adjacent medullary pyramids. These inward cortical extensions are called renal columns or Columns of Bertini.

Final Conceptual Answer: The Columns of Bertini are extensions of the renal cortex that project between the medullary pyramids.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q13 - Structural differences in cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately distinguishes cortical nephrons from juxtamedullary nephrons in the human kidney?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Nephron Subtypes
Based on the depth of the loop of Henle and location of the renal corpuscle, human kidneys contain two types of nephrons: cortical nephrons and juxtamedullary nephrons.

Step 2: Cortical Nephron Features
In the majority (about 85%) of nephrons, termed cortical nephrons, the loop of Henle is short and extends only very little into the medulla. In these nephrons, the vasa recta is absent or highly reduced.

Step 3: Juxtamedullary Nephron Features
In a minority (about 15%) of nephrons, termed juxtamedullary nephrons, the renal corpuscles lie near the corticomedullary junction, and their loops of Henle are very long and run deep into the medulla. They are closely accompanied by hairpin-shaped vasa recta, essential for generating the medullary osmotic gradient.

Final Conceptual Answer: Cortical nephrons have a short loop of Henle extending minimally into the medulla and have reduced or absent vasa recta, whereas juxtamedullary nephrons possess a long loop running deep into the medulla with well-developed vasa recta.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q14 - Vascular pathway through human nephron

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly traces the sequential pathway of blood flow through the microvasculature associated with a nephron?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Arterial Input
Blood enters the kidney via the renal artery, which subdivides into interlobar, arcuate, and interlobular arteries, giving rise to afferent arterioles.

Step 2: Glomerular Capillary Tuft
The afferent arteriole breaks into a high-pressure capillary network called the glomerulus, enclosed within Bowman's capsule.

Step 3: Efferent Vessel and Secondary Capillaries
Instead of a venule, an efferent arteriole carries blood away from the glomerulus. The efferent arteriole then divides into the peritubular capillary network surrounding the convoluted tubules and gives off the hairpin-shaped vasa recta alongside Henle's loop before draining into the venous system.

Final Conceptual Answer: Blood flows sequentially: Afferent arteriole → Glomerular capillaries → Efferent arteriole → Peritubular capillaries and vasa recta → Renal venules.

answer.text: Renal vein → Efferent arteriole → Glomerular capillaries → Afferent arteriole → Peritubular capillaries
Efferent arteriole → Glomerular capillaries → Afferent arteriole → Vasa recta → Renal artery

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q15 - Renal blood flow relative to cardiac output

questiontext.text: On average, how much blood is filtered by the human kidneys per minute, and what fraction of the cardiac output does this represent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Normal Renal Perfusion
Both kidneys receive a very large proportion of the resting systemic cardiac output to perform homeostatic ultrafiltration.

Step 2: Quantitative Evaluation
On average, 1100 to 1200 mL of blood is filtered through the kidneys per minute. Considering a resting cardiac output of approximately 5000 mL/minute from each ventricle, this represents roughly one-fifth (20 to 24%) of the blood pumped out by the heart per minute.

Final Conceptual Answer: 1100-1200 mL/minute is filtered by the kidneys, constituting roughly one-fifth of the cardiac output of each ventricle.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q16 - Standard values of glomerular filtration rate

questiontext.text: What is the normal Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy adult human?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of GFR
Glomerular Filtration Rate is defined as the total volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys combined per unit time.

Step 2: Quantitative Standard
In a healthy adult, GFR is approximately 125 mL per minute. Calculating this over 24 hours: 125 mL/min × 60 min/hour × 24 hours/day = 180,000 mL/day, or 180 litres per day.

Final Conceptual Answer: The normal GFR is approximately 125 mL/minute, corresponding to 180 litres per day.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q17 - Three layers of the glomerular filtration membrane

questiontext.text: Ultrafiltration of blood in the renal corpuscle occurs across a filtration membrane composed of which three structural layers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Filtration Barrier Components
Glomerular filtration occurs across three distinct physical barriers separating capillary blood from the Bowman's space.

Step 2: Sequential Layers
These three layers are: (1) the fenestrated endothelium of the glomerular capillaries, (2) the non-cellular acellular basement membrane shared between the two layers, and (3) the visceral epithelial layer of Bowman's capsule formed by specialized podocytes.

Final Conceptual Answer: The filtration membrane consists of the endothelium of glomerular blood vessels, the basement membrane, and the visceral epithelium of Bowman's capsule.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q18 - Composition of initial glomerular filtrate

questiontext.text: Why is glomerular filtration characterized as a process of ultrafiltration?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Filtration Selectivity
Under the hydrostatic pressure of the glomerular capillaries, blood is filtered so finely through the three-layered filtration barrier that it separates macromolecules from micromolecules.

Step 2: Solute Permeability
Cellular components (erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets) and large plasma proteins (such as albumin and globulins) cannot cross the slit pores and negatively charged basement membrane. Thus, the resulting filtrate contains nearly all plasma solutes (water, glucose, amino acids, ions, urea) except proteins.

Final Conceptual Answer: It is ultrafiltration because virtually all plasma constituents except proteins pass into the lumen of Bowman's capsule.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q19 - Structural arrangement of podocytes and slit pores

questiontext.text: What is the structural role of podocytes in the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cytology of Podocytes
Podocytes are specialized epithelial cells forming the visceral wall of Bowman's capsule wrapped around the glomerular capillaries.

Step 2: Filtration Slits
These cells possess extending interdigitating foot processes (pedicels) that leave tiny gaps called filtration slits or slit pores, through which water and small solutes pass into Bowman's space.

Final Conceptual Answer: Podocytes are intricately arranged to leave minute filtration slits or slit pores for ultrafiltration.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q20 - Quantitative comparison of GFR and urine output

questiontext.text: A healthy human generates approximately 180 litres of glomerular filtrate daily, yet voids only about 1.5 litres of urine. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Volumes
Total volume of filtrate formed per day = 180 L. Total volume of urine released per day = 1.5 L.

Step 2: Percentage Calculation
Volume reabsorbed = 180 L - 1.5 L = 178.5 L. Fraction reabsorbed = (178.5 / 180) × 100% ≈ 99.17%, which is nearly 99 per cent.

Final Conceptual Answer: Nearly 99 per cent of the filtrate is reabsorbed by the renal tubules.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_EXCRETORY_PRODUCTS_AND_THEIR_ELIMINATION_MCQ_Q21 - Anatomy and location of the juxtaglomerular apparatus

questiontext.text: How is the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) anatomically formed in the human kidney?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural Organization of JGA
The juxtaglomerular apparatus is a specialized regulatory microstructural complex located within each nephron.

Step 2: Cellular Components
It is formed by cellular modifications of the distal convoluted tubule (macula densa) and the afferent arteriole (juxtaglomerular granular cells) at the point where the initial part of the DCT contacts the vascular pole of its parent glomerulus.

Final Conceptual Answer: JGA is formed by cellular modifications in the distal convoluted tubule and the afferent arteriole at their location of contact.
